newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania set for fresh crisis over election law.
newsitem.headline: Albania set for fresh crisis over election law.

text.p: Albania was set for a fresh political crisis on Tuesday as parliament passed a law on new elections seen as vital to stop its slide to chaos but which was opposed by most parties in a national unity government.

The elections, expected at the end of June, are a key element of international efforts to prevent Albania sliding once more into the rioting and violence of February and March after the collapse of high-yielding pyramid investment schemes.

The new election law was one of the points of a political contract brokered last week by European envoy Franz Vranitzky which aimed to put back on track the early elections which were called amid the troubles.

The election law passed by parliament was proposed by the former ruling Democratic Party of President Sali Berisha, which has a majority in parliament but was opposed by most parties of a nine-party Government of Reconciliation.
Under the Vranitzky contract, parliament must pass the law so Berisha can call a poll by May 15. Albanian law says the president has to call elections at least 45 days before voting.
The Socialists said that passing the law would plunge Albania once more into crisis and threatened that it and the parties in the government would walk out.

"We will also reconsider our participation in the government and also in the parliament (if the law was passed)," the chairman of the Socialist Party's parliamentary group, Naim Dokle, told parliament.
"The passing of that draft will return the Albanian crisis back to that of before March 1997," he added.
Western diplomats said there was a danger that if the Democrats forced through their own law, other parties would refuse to take part in elections, leading to more chaos.
The Socialists said the election law presented by the Democratic Party conflicted with the Vranitzky deal as it was not approved by the nine-party government.
The Socialists also objected to the proposed division of seats to be decided by proportional and majority voting.

The Democrats want a law that was based on the 1996 elections, where it won 122 out of 140 seats but which was called flawed by international observers and was boycotted by the Socialists on the final day of voting.
The Socialist Party and the rest of the government wanted a law that had more seats decided by proportional representation to allow smaller parties a voice in parliament.
As the politicians argued, officials of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), brokering the talks on the law, were busy trying to find a compromise.
One Western security official said there was disappointment that the Democratic Party had drafted its own law and that intensive talks were being held to clarify the situation.
The Democratic Party insisted that its draft law was in line with the Vranitzky deal.
Another key point of the Vranitzky contract was the disbanding of so-called salvation committees in the south of the country by May 14.
They were set up to restore some kind of order after riots and are only due to meet on May 16.
